utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honour, there are one or two administrative matters. I wonder could they be dealt with perhaps at the end of the day; Your Honour would hear us on one or two matters that don't concern this witness but perhaps other factors in relation to timings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will try to remember that, Mr. Moore. If you think it is obviously escaping my memory at that point, please remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, what is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: My name is Emil Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when were you born, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of January, 1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll try and summarise your educational background. Is it right that you attended elementary school and then you attended secondary medical school in Zagreb from 1949 until 1953; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That you moved to Vukovar in 1958; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then from 1968 until 1972 you had been studying in Belgrade for two years at the medical school for sanitary engineers. I think you did that at the same time that you worked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then you subsequently were working in the Vukovar Hospital and you were involved, I think, with the community of Vukovar which was, I believe, described as regional government? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: First I worked at the medical centre. I was at the lab and blood transfusion ward, or department. After 10 years of work at the hospital, I went to the Vukovar municipality where I was appointed sanitary inspector of the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The work of sanitary inspector, did that involve the examination of such things such as water-supply within the Vukovar municipality area?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in very general terms, what other work did that sanitary inspectorate work involve?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I oversaw health production and manufacturing and also the trade of different foods of animal and biological kind. Also this included the monitoring of the quality of water, combatting the outbreak of infectious diseases. These were the key duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal in very general terms again with the period from, shall we say, August, mid-August, until the fall of Vukovar, which we will ascribe to the 18th of November. Now, I think it's right to say that you were a volunteer and you were working within a -- a medical health capacity for Croatian forces, is that right or not, through that period?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal, if I may, please, with the sort of work you were doing through that two- to three-month period. And I refer to your sanitary work, or your medical work. Did you have any dealings with the -- the water that was being used for drinking in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we deal with the period, shall we say September, October, November, how good was the water-supply in Vukovar for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Up to a certain point good water quality was maintained in hygienic terms. But as there were electricity cuts, the quality of the water became worse and worse, because it was powered by electricity. And even though the waterworks had experts on its staff who checked the quality of water on a daily basis, we as inspectors also carried out these controls but within other institutions that were authorised to do that. We demanded that the water be of excellent condition in order to be used, and for as long as this was possible the waterworks did supply the town with its water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did there come a time when it was necessary to take steps to protect the civilian population from harm from the water-supply?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was wrong with the standard of water in October and November?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: At the time the town water system was not able to transport water through the pipe system because it was pretty damaged. The actual waterworks itself and the labs were also destroyed. So we needed to take some other more simple measures to order or to warn the population that the water that they were using from wells had to be boiled first, meaning they had to disinfect the water thermically. They had to disinfect the water using a means provided for such cases in order to preserve their health.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The sewers themselves that clearly existed in Vukovar, are you able to say if the sewer pipes were damaged as a result of military action?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There wasn't a single building or facility in Vukovar that was undamaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you have sewers or fluid from sewers going into the drinking water and it remains untreated, what sort of illnesses does one then find occurring?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: All sorts of illnesses. There were different types of epidemics caused by the bad quality of the water. There was some other illnesses which spread in the water because these were all infectious diseases with a short term of incubation, but which last a long time. They're both infectious and contagious. They spread quickly, and with any sort of lack of caution it can easily lead to sickness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say that one of the processes that you recommended was thermic. I presume you mean by boiling, is that right, that if you boil water for a period of time, it improves?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To your personal knowledge, was that advice given to the civilian population in Vukovar through this period?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us how that warning or health warning or recommendation was transmitted to the civilian population of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The Vukovar radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what sort of advice was being given over the radio to the population?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Advice was given that water that was used for drinking had to be boiled for at least 10 minutes to kill all the microorganisms that may be in the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were chemicals used at any time to sterilise or clean the water?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, natrum hydrochloride was one of the main agents that was used and that is meant to be used for that purpose in a certain concentration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to deal with the wells in Vukovar. We know and indeed you have mentioned that wells existed in Vukovar. Do you know how or whether the civilian population used those wells through the three-month period?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did use the wells that were not destroyed, because they were deliberately targeted. If you leave a population without water, it means that it will start dying slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say that the wells were being deliberately targeted, how do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: My wife went to get water from a neighbour who had wells. Suddenly shells started falling. Luckily the one that fell closest to the well did not actually hit the well, did not explode.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about one incident, perhaps close to home, if I may use that phrase. Did you have any information that other wells were being targeted, wells that were being used by the civilian population through that period?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you just expand that answer a little?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Vukovar was supplied centrally, so that gradually this centralised network expanded through the years. Many people left their old wells, but they didn't completely abandon them, they sort of conserved them. They covered them up to prevent debris falling inside and to maintain the quality of the water. However, when you needed to use the water again that had been preserved in wells like that for a while, it needed to be disinfected first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about shells landing in the area of the wells?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Some wells were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, please, with one area of your evidence or one other area? You've told us that you were living in Vukovar. Up until the 17th of November in what sort of building were you living?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: At the hospital, the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the period before you go to the hospital. Where did you live before then?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I lived in Borisa Kidrica Street. I don't know what it's called now. It's near the soccer stadium in Vukovar in a kind of depression. These are three buildings four storeys each. I lived on the first floor of the middle building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how safe was it for you to go out of those buildings through September, October and November?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It wasn't safe at all because the buildings were about 400 metres away from the right bank of the Vuka River, and that section of town on the right bank of the Vuka River was occupied and there was constant shooting. I can say that one day - I don't recall the date - an airplane fired a missile or a rocket, which hit an apartment and destroyed it. It was on the ground floor. My wife happened to be on the ground floor as well, but on the other side. She was on the right-hand side, facing the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about the building away from the right bank of the Vuka River, and you described the -- that area as being occupied and constant shooting. What sort of shooting was there, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I would be returning from work, and I'll tell you about one occasion. Three or four metres before I was going to enter the entrance-hall of my building I just happened to move my head and avoided being killed by a grenade or a shell. The shelling was constant. You never knew when it would begin and you never knew when it would stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to move on to the 17th of November because we've heard much evidence about what happened in Vukovar before then. So let us deal with the 17th of November, there or thereabouts. Can you tell us then, please, why it was you went to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It wasn't safe, and a neighbour came to tell me that tanks had arrived, tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army and that they had already crossed the rail tracks. Later I saw them on a slope. That was when my wife and I decided that the best thing to do would be to leave. And we went to the Vukovar Hospital. This was already late at night. It was dark, there were no lights anywhere. We were just about to turn left into street when they began firing. We continued on our way to the hospital. I entered immediately. My wife couldn't go inside right away, but upon the intervention of my colleagues, she also managed to get inside. That day there wasn't a lot of shelling. I mentioned just that one occasion. It was around 10.00 or 11.00, I can't tell you exactly what time this happened. Then it became quiet in Vukovar. Practically that was the day that Vukovar fell. Because all the soldiers had left the fronts that were there, our fronts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with, please, the hospital itself. Now, I know that you will give evidence that you subsequently went into the hospital. So may I just deal with that? Did you enter the hospital complex with your wife or by yourself?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: With my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you went into the hospital, did you see any people that you knew?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I knew many people. I had worked there for 10 years. Milicko Zuvic, Milenko Zugic, Ivankovic, Adam. Those were the colleagues that I used to work with and they were there. Ivankovic came a little bit later after us. Stjepan Guncevic also came there, he arrived a day later. There were many people. We all were at the X-ray ward. We slept in the dark room where the film was developed. We spent time together, in a strange way, because all of us had had something strange happen to us. We didn't expect anything like that to happen in our former country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How would you describe the atmosphere in the hospital at that time when you went in?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was very unpleasant, the atmosphere. There was a mass of people standing in the yard. Only a few could actually go inside. The number of people in the yard was maybe from 1.000 to 2.000 or more. I don't know if anyone managed to actually count how many people there were, but I believe that there were at least a thousand people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I ask you if you actually saw anyone called Marin Vidic or sometimes known as Bili Vidic. Did you see him at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him at the hospital. Before that we worked together at the Vukovar municipality. I also worked together with him during shelling. We went to Borovo in order to take some hygienic and epidemiological measures in order to prevent an outbreak of diseases. So I worked with him. I also saw him at the hospital before the fall of Vukovar. I went to see him personally and we talked. I had a special pass from the Croatian Red Cross to be able to participate in the negotiations. However, when I showed this pass once at Velepromet, they tore it and they told me where I could put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, just dealing with the hospital, can you remember your -- your first recollection of the arrival of either JNA soldiers, either regular or irregular?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was easy to enter the hospital. I don't know if there was any shooting; I couldn't hear that from the dark room where I was. But it was easy to get in. I don't think that there were any problems until the evacuation of the population began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's my fault for phrasing it perhaps the way I did. Can you remember the arrival of JNA soldiers coming to the hospital? And if you can, can you tell us, as far as you can remember, when that was?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: This was on the 18th and 19th. It was the morning of the -- from the 18th to the 19th when they came to get Marin Vidic, Bili. A major, Mr. Sljivancanin, and an escort of his whom I knew as Bogdan Kuzmic who I think used to work at the hospital reception. Major Sljivancanin entered Vidic's office, I don't know what they talked about. Probably to agree to a surrender. Even though I spent a lot of time with Marin Vidic we never spoke about that directly. Kuzmic stood at the door. After a certain amount of time they went, they left the hospital and I didn't see Marin Vidic all the time until Sremska Mitrovica when I began to -- an operation to disinfect the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you could see, who was in charge of the JNA presence at that time? If you can't assist us, do say so.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was one of the people who was in charge of all those actions starting from taking Marin Vidic, Bili, away. Then other soldiers began to arrive in Yugoslav People's Army uniforms. We were ordered to leave the rooms where we were staying because we were medical -- we were not members of the medical personnel. The medical personnel had their own meeting. I don't know how they resolved this matter. We had to go out into the yard. There were these two soldiers in the yard. We had to line up. There was some words used, quote/unquote, there were curses used, and then after a certain amount of time we had to take everything out of our pockets, place it in front of us to show what we had on us. When this was finished, well, actually it was still underway, we were exposed to curses. They cursed our parents, something that is not really fitting for anyone to use. After that buses were parked in front of the entrance to the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's quite a long answer. I'm going to try and break it into parts, if I may. In fairness, I think it 's right to say you did not know the name of Major Sljivancanin at that time, and you say you saw him with Bogdan Kuzmic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. It's like this: I think all of Vukovar knew Major Sljivancanin. He was quite a notorious military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, can you describe then, please, the -- can you describe the height of the person that you say was Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was a person who was, I thought, 180 centimetres tall, but later when I actually saw him, I observed he might be even taller. He had black hair, he wore a moustache, and he always wore a JNA army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the hat that he would wear, can you remember what sort of hat he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. A Tito cap with a five-pointed star. He said that he represented the JNA, and that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What sort of attitude did Major Sljivancanin demonstrate to people when he was dealing with them in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was an extrovert, in my opinion. He refused to take criticism from anyone. He was an operations officer who probably following somebody else's orders, or on his own initiative, carried out his tasks as best he could. I have a high regard of him as a soldier, but not as a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can we just perhaps set aside your personal views on Major Sljivancanin, just deal with the evidence, if you would be so kind. Let's deal with the two soldiers who were in the yard. Now, are you able to say whether they were regular soldiers or TO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I learned later on, because those same two soldiers escorted us to Sremska Mitrovica, that their names were Pero, that was one of them, I don't know his last name, and he hailed from Bosnia, from a village called Josavka, it's more to the west or well near the tri-apartheid border where I had passed on the motorway so I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My question that I asked you, if you are able to do so, are you able to say whether they were regular soldiers, regular JNA, what I call conscripts, or whether they were TO soldiers who were searching you at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I think and believe that they were members of the JNA because they wore the same kind of uniforms that the Yugoslav army soldiers wore. And I wouldn't say they were territorials because they escorted us as far as Sremska Mitrovica from Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with the buses. You've told us that there were buses. Now, how many buses do you remember now as being outside that hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you clearly went on a bus.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I hadn't quite got there, but thank you for answering the question in any event.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. Not a problem. How many people were on the bus when it moved off; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Altogether there were about 200 people. I'm sure of 207, then there were some who were saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about just your bus. I want to try and focus now just on your bus and not what we see around. If I do I'll mention that --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So let's deal with your bus. How many people do you think were in your bus, the bus that you travelled?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: About 40. I can't tell you the precise number because I didn't count, but it was around 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And of the people that you knew on that bus, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Like this: All of us were Croats. I don't know about Berghofer because he has a German-sounding last name, but I think he declared himself as a Croat; however, I'm not certain about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again the bus that you travelled on, how many women were on that bus that you could see?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I think there was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal then, please, with the bus moving off. We know from evidence that the buses went to the JNA barracks. So can I just deal with the trip, please, from the hospital to the barracks only. When you were travelling in your bus, to get to the JNA barracks you must cross a bridge over the Vuka River. I think that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were travelling over the bridge on the Vuka River, were you able to see any of the other bridges?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you see anything occurring on any of the other bridges that caught your attention?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you very slowly, please, tell us what it is you saw occurring on the other bridge or bridges?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We were on the right-hand bridge looking downstream. The bridge you're asking me about was the second bridge towards the Danube across the River Vuka. There was a building there which used to be a confectionery and it was very close to the bridge. Should I go on? There I saw several persons. I thought that one of them was Mr. Vance, but it wasn't Mr. Vance; it was someone who resembled him. I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you saw this, as you thought, Mr. Vance, presumably a civilian, was that person alone or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. He was escorted by Major Sljivancanin and this man whom I thought was Mr. Vance was there, and maybe someone else. But they were standing between the bridge and that house. I was on their left-hand side and in the bus and so I was able to observe that from the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether you were able to identify if there were any soldiers apart from Major Sljivancanin? I'm not asking that you were able to say who they are, just if military personnel were there.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then deal, please, with the trip across the bridge and moving on to the JNA barracks. Now, do you remember arriving at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what happened when you arrived at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Before entering the barracks we saw several corpses in the direction of the health centre. I don't know who the dead people were or who had killed them. Before entering the building of the barracks the gate was open and the buses went in one by one. I was in the third bus, and this was also the third bus to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you any idea what time it was that you arrived at the barracks? And please don't guess.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I wasn't wearing a watch. But I assume it was around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the bus that you were travelling on to the JNA barracks? Can you remember any of the names of people who were on that bus with you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Berghofer, Guncevic, a man called Veliki Bojler, Damjan Samardzic. There were people I knew and people I didn't know. There was also a lady, I think. And there were a lot of people there whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us deal, please, then, with the bus itself. Again, we have heard that the buses stopped within the precincts of the JNA barracks. Did you see anybody outside the buses when you had parked or stopped?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough to tell us, please, exactly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I saw a soldier wearing a military uniform whom I had seen before he arrived in barracks preparing food in a school for everyone who had been mobilised. They were still volunteers at that point; they were actually mobilised much later. This man hails from Bobota. That's a place some 15 kilometres or less away from Vukovar in the direction of Osijek. Near the Vupik administrative building you have to turn right. He was standing guard in the barracks. There was a big roof and there were lots of weapons underneath it. If someone had activated a single grenade, I think it would have blown up half of Vukovar. Before all this his wife had come to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not a problem. Did you see anybody else apart from the man who cooked for the reservists?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw persons who spoke with a different kind of accent and they were wearing little round caps. These caps had something on them, and only later on did I learn that they were called Topola. We'll maybe come back to them. I saw -- the caps had braids on them. Let me just try to remember. The last name might come back to me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Don't worry about the names. Let's just deal with the general picture and then we'll try and tighten down on detail. I'm sorry, there seems to be a problem. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could the Prosecutor ask the witness again about these men with little round caps? The man had said that the caps were round with some kind of braid on them, and that these were poplar trees, or Topola. Could the Prosecutor clarify this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well I hope I'm not going to clarify unless I'm absolutely forced to do so because my learned friend will have ample opportunity to do that in cross-examination, I'm sure. I want to try and keep the witness giving evidence in a particular direction, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal with the number of people that you saw in the barracks outside the buses? Can we deal with that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were people from Vukovar, but also foreigners, people we didn't know. These were persons with whom I had worked in Ovcara once upon a time, Inka, her husband Vlado, then the Sreto I have just mentioned who was guarding those weapons. Many people came to see us, to see what all this looked like. Vlado Kosic, Inka's husband, said, "Emil, choose a good bus," and I asked him which was a better bus, and he said, "Well, they're all the same." He was kind of joking, but it was all serious at the same time. It gave us food for thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask: The people who were outside the buses, people that you've described, did you see any of them wearing uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vlado Kosic and his wife had military uniforms, and the man guarding the weapons was also wearing a military uniform, with all the insignia of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And how were those people behaving, the people who were outside the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They were laughing at us. When he told me I hadn't chosen a good bus, I began to understand. I had an idea of what might happen. And that's exactly what did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know there are ladies present, and I know you don't like swearing in their presence, or indeed at all, but can you remember the sort of things that they were saying?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We Croats had suddenly become Ustashas, according to them. They cursed our Ustasha mothers and fathers. They threatened us. They told us we would not fare well. I had the impression that they knew our destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with, again, just your bus only? Can you remember if anyone in uniform or indeed perhaps not even in uniform, if anyone got on to your bus at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. One or two soldiers got on, and asked whether there was anyone on the bus who was an employee of the medical centre. My friend Guncevic was sitting nearby, said, "Yes, I have a card showing that I am an employee of the medical centre." He showed it to that person, but that person didn't accept the card because there was no photograph on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How did you feel about the way they were behaving and the things that they were saying to you and the other people in the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Humiliated. Embarrassed, very bad. I began to reach conclusions about those people and the way they were treating others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what conclusions were you coming to?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That they didn't wish us well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you've said that one or two soldiers got on and asked if anyone on the bus was an employee of the medical centre. The person or persons who got on to the bus, clearly you say were soldiers. Are you able to say if they had any rank, whether they were what I will call officers or non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is leading. The witness said two soldiers got on, and previously in his testimony he always drew a distinction between people who were soldiers and not, and I think that the Prosecutor is now trying to lead the witness and get him to change his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic, I don't agree with your contention. "Soldiers" is a term often used only of the lowest rank but equally of anybody who is a member of the armed force. Are you under control? You were coughing. Yes. And this question is not leading to any particular answer, but inquiring whether the soldiers seen were of any particular rank within the armed force. Carry on, please, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us with that, Mr. Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In my view, privates, non-commissioned officers, and commissioned officers are all soldiers. In the barracks there were -- or, rather, on the bus there were two soldiers asking who had a card. I didn't have a card, so I didn't say anything. A card of the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much indeed. How long do you think you stayed at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Until about 1400 hours. Please don't hold me to it precisely, but that was the approximate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then deal with the bus or buses leaving the JNA barracks. We again have heard evidence, and I know that you will give such evidence, that the bus went from the barracks to Ovcara. Can you please deal with that area of evidence? Now, did the buses leave together or one by one; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In the meantime another bus entered the barracks compound. We didn't know where it was from and why it was there. I can't say whether it left before us or after us, because our heads were looking at the ground. These were frequent instructions given to us, that we should look down. This was the sixth bus that came into the barracks yard. We never found out what the fate of that bus was. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. You've told us that you were given frequent instructions that you should look down. Who gave you those instructions to look down?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were two soldiers in the bus. I think that they were just regular soldiers, conscripts, wearing JNA uniforms. They started to mistreat us. If you have rings, if you have gold, if you have money, you should give all of that to us for safe-keeping and then when you come back we will give it back to you. One of them was from Bosnia, I know that for sure. These were young men. I think that they had just arrived, I mean they were just at the beginning of their regular military term of duty. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with Ovcara and the arrival at Ovcara, if I may. Do you remember the bus coming to the hangar at Ovcara and stopping?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it covered the road to Negoslavci, before it got to Negoslavci it turned left and that road leads to Ovcara as well. Actually, the main road that leads to Ovcara goes in the direction of Ilok and Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, and I'm going to try and break it into parts as I normally do, can you tell us, then, about getting off the bus? Did that occur, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The buses came in a certain order and that was the order in which the people from the bus disembarked. The bus would come in front of the hangar and the people on it would disembark in such a way that they had to pass through a gauntlet before getting to the hangar door. There were Chetniks there as well as prominent people from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with your arrival at Ovcara? You say that you came out. You've described a gauntlet. I'll deal with that in a moment. But did you see any persons in a JNA -- or JNA uniform outside the hangar in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I was in the third bus and that we had started to descend from the third bus when I saw actually what was awaiting us. One man was waiting for us as we were getting off the bus, and he was going through our pockets asking for money. He didn't search me, but he saw my glasses, which were light-sensitive. The sun was going down a bit, and the lenses went a little bit dark. He seemed to like my glasses, he took them, tried them on so that they didn't fit so he threw them down to the ground. This man was wearing a uniform of the JNA, but I could see that it was too tight for him. He couldn't button it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, you have told us about a JNA soldier, perhaps a little too large for his uniform. Did you see any JNA soldiers where the uniform seemed to fit?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: These were soldiers who had come in our escort, these first ones. Secondly, when we were passing through this gauntlet, I saw my one-time friend, Slavko Dokmanovic. We had worked together at the municipal offices at one time. We even spent time together. He called out, "Oh, look, it's our inspector. Emil, you're here as well. What are you doing there?" I said, "What could I be doing? I'm doing what everyone is doing, getting off the bus and going to the hangar." They were beating people severely; men were just falling down. There were all sorts of people there from Territorial Defence of Vukovar also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the type of beating and the nature and severity of the beating. I know you don't like discussing it, but would you please tell the Court as precisely as you can the sort of beatings that were being given and whether any weapons were being used?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I have to name the people so that you could tell who is who. Slavko Dokmanovic was there, people from the Vukovar Territorial Defence were there. They were using bats for the beating. Some were using their weapons. They were also kicking people. They were actually using whatever they had, including their fists, their feet. I'm talking about that space from the bus to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did anybody fall to the ground as a result of the beating?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was already happening at the hangar. Damjan Samardzic fell; his nickname was Veliki Bojler. Another person whose name was Kemal. They were entering the hangar and they killed them with their kicks. They were beating them. They were first of all lying on their back and then they were lying on stomach, both Kemal and Damjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I want to deal just with the gauntlet, before we get to the hangar, all right? So let's just deal with the gauntlet before anybody goes into the hangar. So dealing with that -- what I will call the path to the hangar, you know the gauntlet was either side, did you see anybody fall to the ground when they were going through the gauntlet only?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was probably already inside, and we were not able to look back. I didn't look back. You needed to get into the hangar as soon as possible because the beating was pretty severe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How severely were you beaten? You, yourself.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Dokmanovic did not hit me, but he provoked others so that they would know my first and last name, and when he said, "Inspector" they probably thought I was some sort of police inspector. Had he not called out my name, I don't think I would have had such a bad time of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how bad a time of it you had? Can you describe to the Court, tell them how severely you were beaten? Do you mind doing that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Everyone was covered with blood. I hadn't seen such a beating anywhere. Only in the movies. They really fell upon us, including the members of the Territorial Defence. And I think had somebody not said that the colonel was coming, they would have really worked us over terribly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We'll come to the phrase about the colonel coming. Let me just deal finally with the following piece, or the following question. You've mentioned persons in the gauntlet, the Vukovar TO defence, Dokmanovic. Did you see anybody in JNA uniform in that gauntlet or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Dokmanovic was wearing a JNA uniform. He was wearing rank insignia; he was either a lieutenant-colonel or a major. He had a blue uniform, a Tito cap with a five-pointed star on his head. He arrived as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many people were either side of you when you entered? How many people were in the gauntlet? Can you give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: About 12 to 13 people on each side. So twice the number. It was 12 to 13 people on each side, perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to go on to the actual hangar itself when you go inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before I ask any questions, might I inquire of the Court if this would be an appropriate time or would Your Honour wish me to continue? This is quite a good break point for a witness to give evidence. The only thing that I would ask is if I'm going to deal with the hangar, that I deal with the hangar in toto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Moore, it's a little early and runs us into some tightness later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the hangar itself. You've told us about the hangar. Did you actually know the Ovcara hangar before that day?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I passed by the hangars at least 100 times, because there was a fishpond there and I used to go there for fishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, please, with your entry into the hangar? You've told us that you had gone through the gauntlet and the various beatings. When you went into the hangar, had you been injured in the beatings at the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this repeated itself in the hangar as well. Milos, not Milan Bulic, actually took the crutch from one of the people who were wounded. His name was Dado, and he hit me twice on the neck with that crutch, and I fell. I got up and I went after him; however, he had already moved on to a different place. As far as my vertebrae on my neck is concerned, I still have problems to this very day. I always have to go and have my neck adjusted and it's very painful, and every time it begins to hurt, it always reminds me of the terrible time that I had when I got that injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just to assist the Court, we will be seeking leave to put an exhibit before the Court, namely, this witness's -- or a medical examination of this witness in 1992 and the injuries that we say were caused in Ovcara and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, please, with what you saw inside the hangar? How many people were inside that hangar; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There was about 207 people. This is a number that we came to by compiling the information for ourselves. The people who had entered the hangar before us had to lean directly against the wall with their arms and legs spread and the hands were touching the wall while the feet were away from the wall. And that was the position that they were in as we were entering the hangar. When they started to beat us, not only by the people there, but others, all of them who were there were inflicting blows. They were certainly lacking in humanity. There was some straw in one corner. We went and sat on that straw, and I could see that people were trying to clean the blood off. And that's where we were waiting to see what would happen to us next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us earlier on about two individuals that you saw attacked, and you mentioned specifically Samardzic, and I think Kemo.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Kemal and Samardzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, please, with what you saw occurring with Samardzic. Will you tell the Court, please, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Samardzic entered the hangar after me, and he left the bus after I did. So as he was passing through the gauntlet of the people who were beating us they entered the hangar and then they fell upon them. I think that both of them were dead within a couple of minutes. They were beating them on the head, the back, then they placed them on their stomach and then they jumped on them. I think that that is a terrible death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you say that "they" were beating them on the head. Who were "they"?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The people who were in the gauntlet and then there were also some members of the Territorial Defence who came inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about Kemal? How was he attacked?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In the same way that Damjan Samardzic was attacked. There was no longer any time to actually look. It was necessary to find a space where you could protect yourself. We didn't even look that much because it was important to save your own head. Those who had been beaten on the head were unfortunate. All of us were fleeing inside the hangar and were trying to protect our head. Perhaps I wouldn't have sustained such a blow to my neck had not the person who hit me -- I keep forgetting, Milos, Milan Vujic, he came up to me from the back and hit me on the neck from the back. That's when I fell and then I stood up and I ran after him. I probably would have gotten into a fight with him, but he had already gone outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a good thing you didn't get into a fight with him. But let's just deal with the situation in the hangar. These attacks that you have described to -- of other attacks as well, did you see anyone trying to stop these attacks being carried out on you? Not just you personally, but you as a group?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember if you saw anyone wearing a JNA uniform inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But only after the officers came. There was one soldier who was guarding the hangar. He was wearing a JNA uniform. I knew him. He's the son of a certain Marijana who worked with me at the municipal office. He kept opening and closing the hangar door when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that you did see people wearing JNA uniforms, but the phrase that you used was, "But only after the officers came." So can you tell us, please, in your words, about the officers coming to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Someone rushed into the hangar, and I don't know who it was, and they said a colonel and two lieutenant-colonels were coming. I think that he even said the colonel's last name, but I can't be sure about that. In any case, when they arrived, there was silence in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you've said, "When they arrived." Can you just tell us, please, about their arrival and what happened as far as you can remember it, having been hit around the head?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first thing I thought was that these were educated people who had completed high military schools, who had been taught about humane conduct and that they would prevent that, and they did prevent it for a minute. All of those who were in the hangar, they all fled outside. Only the soldier remained who was actually guarding the hangar entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did you then see? You said that it prevented it, but only for a minute. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: At that point perhaps a little bit before the officers entered the hangar, Stevan Zoric came. His nickname was Cevo. And he told me to come, to move from the straw. I went up to him and I said, "Well, you're not going to kill me?" He said, "No, you did a lot for me, and you did it when I needed it most and I'm going to save you." And he took me outside. The officers hadn't arrived yet. I was outside, and then Guncevic and all seven of us, actually, were being brought outside. We were taken out into the yard, and we were standing a little bit off to the side from the hangar entrance, and that was when the JNA officers entered the hangar. We saw everything that was going on in the hangar at that time. Suddenly the hangar doors closed, this was a tin sliding door, and then we heard terrible moaning and wailing. If you permit me, I just wanted to say something else. Do you permit me? Before the officers entered the hangar a man came, I've never seen such a fat and such a large man. He had a real cockade on his cap. He had some sort of rubber bat that was very flexible. He was wearing hand-grenades on him and other things. And he seemed to have a thing for Stef Guncevic. There was a major of the JNA next to him, and he said, "Give me that electric prod so that I can kill this man." And that Chetnik, the person wearing the Chetnik clothing said, "Don't. There's a lot of people watching." Then when they announced that the colonel and two lieutenant-colonels were coming, at that moment all the members of the TO and all of those who were in the hangar just for no reason fled outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about being taken outside, and you have told us about the door sliding closed and hearing moaning inside. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That's when all of us had been brought outside. All seven of us had been taken outside again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what I want to know is this: You've told us about, as you believed, JNA officers arriving. When you were taken outside, had the JNA officers arrived or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They arrived, I was taken outside. All of us who had been taken outside returned into the hangar to see what was going on. Then they asked about us. I was closest to him, and I said to him that some lads had saved us and then he made a list of us. He asked who had saved us, how we knew him, he asked me who I was, the date of my birth and place of residence. He noted all this down on a piece of paper for each one of us and he kept those pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you all right? Is your neck still causing problems?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I'm all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: My neck is painful, but I can stand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can break now or when you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just ask one or two questions, if Your Honour doesn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about the officers, and then you've referred to -- and you used the words "he asked who had saved," and you keep referring to a "he", but you haven't told us who "he" is. Can you tell us who that person is or whether he had a uniform or any rank?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He did not have rank. He was a soldier. He had the military jacket, but his trousers were different. The trousers were not the same colour as far as I can remember. They didn't seem to go with the jacket. And he said to me that he was saving me because I had once done him some sort of big favour. Later on I assumed, and I stress I assume, that I had helped him get sanitary approval before he had been given an appointment or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I'm going to -- we're going to adjourn now, with His Honour's leave. And then when we return I'm going to ask you questions about the JNA officers who had arrived. Do you follow? But we'll do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes past, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we now deal, please, with the hangar and you told us about, I think, three officers coming. So, when did they arrive, please? Just in general sequence.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime around 3.30 or 4.00 [as interpreted]. It was already dark at 5.00, and it was still daylight when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On page 32, line 3 of the transcript I thought the witness said they had come between 3.00 and 3.30, whereas in the transcript it says 3.30 or 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, we've got a small problem with our electronic machine which records our evidence. Can you remember approximately what time these officers came? You've told us that it got dark at about -- it was already dark at 5.00. When did they come?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We set out there -- I'm really trying hard. It was impossible to determine the precise time. I can only give you approximate times. One must understand we were all concerned with staying alive. We weren't asking ourselves what time it was to the minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I think the Court understand. But let's then deal with the officers. So when they came, was it daylight or was it dark?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was still daylight. It was still daylight, yes. But it was towards the end of the day, so it was already beginning to grow a little dark. That was at the time of year when nights are longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, then, please, how you were aware about officers arriving?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Somebody on the outside probably said to someone that the officers were coming, and all the paramilitaries who were in the hangar at that time all disappeared together with territorials. They simply vanished, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I want to focus on is the officers. Did you see the officers arrive?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw them arrive and enter the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many officers as you have described them, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: One colonel and two lieutenant-colonels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how were you able to assess or work out that one was a colonel and two were lieutenant-colonels?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The colonel had epaulets with a golden edge and three stars. The lieutenant-colonels also had a golden edge around the epaulet, but only two stars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you remember what sort of hat or head-gear they were wearing? Please don't guess if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They had Tito caps with five-pointed stars. These were the insignia of the normal JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, what those three officers did when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: When they went in it was very quiet inside. People thought that what had been happening up to that point would stop. There was no one from among the paramilitaries, as I have already said, because they had all left. The officers spoke to those of us who had been saved who had received the guarantee from someone, and as I have already said, he made a list of us all, first and last name, date of birth, father's name, and then we left the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, let's deal with the three officers who arrived. Were there any other soldiers who arrived with the officers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you say that you were spoken to, or "the officers spoke to those of us who had been saved." Can you remember when --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- or where that occurred? Was that inside the hangar or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We spoke only inside the hangar. There was a small table, and the colonel, it was the colonel who did it himself, he used that table to write on. And now I'm ready for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many people did he speak to when he was at the table? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was standing more than sitting at that table, and he spoke to me for only about a minute, or maybe seven to eight minutes, but that sounds like a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: After he had spoken to you, what did you do or where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: When the conversation was over, we left the hangar. One of the officers had probably summoned a vehicle from Vukovar. It was already beginning to grow dark. We were escorted to a Citroen-make car. Near that car I met someone I knew who was the driver. There were two soldiers properly dressed in the regulation JNA uniform, and this man Mile Bakic recognised me and he asked me what I was doing there. And I said, "well, the same as everybody else." And he said, "Well, come and sit next to me." He sat in the driver's seat, I sat next to him. On the right-hand side there was a soldier with a gun. There were, in fact, two soldiers, the second one sat behind with the other men. Six men were behind and the soldier. In front was the soldier, Bakic and myself in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I have a number of questions I want to ask. I'll just deal with the car and then return to the hangar. You've told us about the Citroen, I think your described it, and you told us about two soldiers in it. Are you able to tell us the age of the soldiers who were in that vehicle? Are you able to say whether they were regular JNA or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: These soldiers, judging by their clothes, were members of the regular JNA units. That's what regular soldiers looked like. As for Bakic, well, it was getting dark, but I think he was wearing civilian clothes. I couldn't swear to that, but I have that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about the colonel speaking to you at the table, and he was speaking to you inside the hangar. How long did you remain at the hangar before you left Ovcara in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: When he had taken down our names and details, we went out of the hangar, one by one. And then we waited for all of us to gather together. And then we were called by someone and I can't recall who now. And then we were taken several metres, I don't know how many, to that vehicle. I think it may have been the soldiers who were in the vehicle who escorted us to the vehicle, but I can't be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: From the time that you were taken -- or you went away from the table and you went outside and then a group of you came together, you had told us earlier on that you had believed that the beatings had stopped. Are you able to say whether any of the beatings resumed when the officers were there? I'm not talking about what you had been told; I just want to ask about the period when you were outside.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. From the time when these high-ranking officers arrived and we went out, there was silence. The doors of the hangar were closed. Some men with helmets had arrived, I don't know how many, in a special vehicle, and they went in. They were carrying bats, and then the parade began. They started beating men until they fell down. I don't know how many were killed, but I believe that more than a few were killed. You could hear screams from afar, even though the hangar was closed. And it was horrible. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about men in helmets going in and beating, and the screams. How long did that go on for? Are you able to help us? The screams and the beating.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They were probably divided into two groups. One group was resting and the other group was beating. But I couldn't tell you for how long. I wasn't focusing on that. It's hard to say. If you're between life and death, it's hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, with the names of the people who travelled in the vehicle with you? Now, do you know the names of some of the people who travelled that evening with you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: To Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we get it absolutely right, perhaps I'll rephrase the question. You've told us about going in a van and being escorted with two regular soldiers. You told us there were seven. Can you tell us the names of the people? Is that an easier way?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cakalic, Stjepan Guncevic, Tihomir Perkovic, Vlado Dudas, Zarko Kojic, Tihomir Perkovic. That's seven of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps I had better recount because that isn't seven for me. There is yourself, Mr. Guncevic, Mr. Kojic --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Berghofer, Kojic, Berghofer, Vlado Dudas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have -- I have six names. I will repeat them and if you -- don't guess if you can't remember. There is yourself, Mr. Guncevic, Mr. Berghofer, Mr. Kojic, Mr. Perkovic and Mr. Dudas. If you can't remember any other names, don't worry about that. Let's move on and set that aside, shall we? Now, you are in the vehicle, and where did that vehicle go to, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That vehicle went towards Velepromet in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you got to Velepromet, did you actually go inside the Velepromet facility or not? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We stopped in front of the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you go in?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. But without the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened at Velepromet? Did you stay there or did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who had escorted us to there said they were leaving us to them and that if the soldiers did not come by 7.00 a.m. the following morning they had to kill them -- kill us. The commander who was there, he was from Negoslavci, I knew him. He had taken some exams with me. He said, "No, I am not going to kill them, and you are not going to leave them here. Go to Modateks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's move on to Modateks. Did you go on to Modateks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at Modateks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was dark. That was a company that made clothes and the halls were full of sewing-machines. They put us in a room where there were over a hundred women. There were also elderly people there lying on stretchers, women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how long did you stay at Modateks, then, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I think we spent two nights there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us then when you left Modateks, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Back to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you went back to Velepromet, what happened at Velepromet, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They took us from Modateks. We were escorted by a man who had been tasked to do that, and the man also arrived from Vukovar whom I knew, they took us to Velepromet. And in front of Velepromet there were some people, I don't know how many, across the road. We came by the road and they were on the other side of the road and they started yelling, "Give me Berghofer, give me Cakalic, give me this one or that one. We want to kill them." I knew one of them, and I said, "You should be ashamed of yourself." But he pretended he didn't hear me. We went into Velepromet. They took us toward the death room. That's what that room was called because all kinds of things happened there. It was a carpentry workshop belonging to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what I'm going do is I'm going to have, I hope produced electronically, an aerial photograph of Velepromet. It is number 04672115. It is a photograph the that Court has seen before. Now, can that be displayed, please? I'm hoping that it can be shown on e-court because I want to use the magic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, do you have in front of you -- Mr. Cakalic, the microphone is being blocked, I see, for you. I don't know if you'll be able to be heard. Now just before you put pen to pencil [sic], can I just explain to you, just one moment. We have a photograph of Velepromet. Can you see it clearly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The road is to the right that goes from Vukovar to Negoslavci, the entrance is to the right. Now, are you able to put a large circle around the area where you believe the room of death was located? Can you do that? Now, the pen, if you just draw on it. Try again.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you would just put the pen down, please, and we'll mark that as an A. Perhaps a capital A, would that be possible for someone to do that? Yes, or the usher will help you, I'm sure, to put an A.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And might I make application for that to be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 265.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could that photograph now be, please, removed from the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mine has disappeared; I hope yours has disappeared as well, Mr. Cakalic. Now, let's deal, please, with the room of death as you have described it. Is it still there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's deal, then, with what happened at Velepromet. Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We were at Velepromet until approximately midnight. Many people were taken out there. They were killed. Tihomir Perkovic was killed. Also the director of the Vukovar abattoir, Karlo Crk, Martin Sajtovic and his son were killed. Tihomir Perkovic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, please, with the Velepromet facility and who controlled the facility at that time. Did you see anyone with uniforms controlling the Velepromet facility or within the Velepromet facility? Are you able to remember or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I saw Dr. Mico Maric. He was somewhat concealed. I know that one of our people whom I saw at Velepromet was suffering from diabetes and he was feeling unwell. So he gave him a little bit of sugar. He was almost in a hypoglycemic coma, so he gave him some sugar. Please, could you repeat the question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm sure it was the way I put it. When you were put in the room of death, did anybody guard the room of death?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, two soldiers guarded it. There was the entrance, you saw the windows. The entrance was next to the windows. There was some rooms to the right side and the death room was on the left side. These soldiers robbed us of everything that we had. Soldiers. They took our personal documents, money, they took everything, everything, and destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were these the only soldiers that you saw at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were also those in uniforms, but I knew that they weren't soldiers, because I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you refer to the two soldiers who guarded the room of death, what sort of uniform were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Typical soldiers' uniforms. A cap, Tito-style cap with a five-pointed star, a belt, jacket, rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether they were regular JNA soldiers or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say. However, they were dressed like regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about the age of these soldiers? Are you able to say if they were old, middle-aged or young?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They were young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about people being taken out from the room of death. Who was being taken out from the room of death? Can I just withdraw that question, because it's a silly question. There's my apologies. The room of death, when you went in, were there any other people in that room or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The people that you knew, what ethnicity were they within that room of death?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: You mean the captured people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the people who were taking them out, can you tell us what sort of people were removing the Croats from that room and killing them, as you say?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Usually first the doors would open, a person dressed in a JNA uniform was -- he was in the JNA but he also worked at Vuteks, he wore hand-grenades on either side, he also had a belt, and he actually had two rifles, two automatic rifles with short barrels. That was a certain Zarko; I knew him very well. When he would leave, they would lock the door again. There was a padlock there, so after a certain amount of time the doors would be unlocked again and then so-and-so would be called out and then so-and-so and then so-and-so. Tihomir Perkovic who had gone through this whole parade with us together was taken out and brought back in three times. The fourth time they took him out he never returned. I never heard anything of him, and I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that the people were taken outside and killed. Well, how do you know they were killed?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I heard of Karlo Crk because if you recall he was under just the windows in the room that I described. So Karlo Crk was taken out, and right in front of the door the person who was waiting for him talked to him. He said, "Karlo, what was the situation at the abattoir, what happened to the money what happened to this, what happened to that." They were talking about sort of superficial things and then you heard a bang [as interpreted] and then a noise and then I never heard of Karlo Crk again. He was an agronomy engineer, and he was the director of the Vukovar abattoir and I never heard of him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The other people that you saw taken out, the people that you knew that were not brought back, did you ever see them again?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have another intervention to the transcript. It's page 43, line 6. The witness said that then he heard a blow, and that he never saw that person again. In the transcript it says [In English] "Bang." [Interpretation] A bang, which seems to me can mean several things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you about Karlo Crk? It's just to help us with the documents that are created. I just want to deal with that again very briefly. You say that you saw -- or knew that Karlo was outside, he had been taken outside. He had been asked about the situation at the abattoir, and you said --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I heard that he was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that you heard a noise. Now, one person has heard "blow," one person has heard "bang." Can you help us, whether it was a blow or whether it was a bang? Well, I see my learned friends grimacing, but I don't know see why they are grimacing, because I am dealing with the point I hope, perfectly fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So are you able to help me with that, or to help the Court with that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I heard a blow. You can sort of perceive it in a way. It was a blow, a whack, a slap, and I never heard anything of him again. I know later that he was buried and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. May I thank Mr. Vasic for that. Now, can we deal, then, please, with the room that you were in. How long did you remain in that room? Have you any idea?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Until midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us then how you were removed from the room or how you were taken out of the room?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: A captain came, Captain Kosa. He entered the room. He sort of mingled with us, and he said, "Come on, men. Go out. I am here with a bus to get you, and if you don't go out, the Chetniks will come and they'll slaughter you all." I asked him to give his officers's word, which is what he did and then we believed him. We went outside. Well, you know what we needed to do first. Our bladders were full. And then after that, with this captain, we followed him to the bus which was a little bit at a distance from us. I don't know how many metres. We entered the bus, and they tried to turn the ignition on, but the motor wouldn't start, and then they made another attempt. And then he said, "Well, let's go out and push the bus and then it will -- the ignition will go on." That's what we did. We pushed, the engine was turned on. And we didn't even reach the door, and the Chetniks had already started singing their songs, they'll be meat or flesh, their usual songs.
