Slobo, Slobo, send us some salad, there will be meat, we're slaughtering Croats, that was the sort of thing that they were singing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you are in a bus that eventually works. And where did you end up? Where did the bus go to?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: To the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us very briefly, please, what happened at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Nothing. We were received well by young conscripts. They gave us something to eat, we were hungry, they gave us water. They behaved properly towards us. We talked amongst ourselves a lot. Then they put us in a room. Some more senior soldiers came to that room later. I don't know what their position was, but they started slowly to slap some men. They didn't touch me, but I saw them do it to others. They spoke in a strange accent. I don't think that they were from that area. And I don't think that they were from Slavonia at all. This went on all night. They untied a man's hands which had been tied with some sort of wire. We tried that already in the room of death, but it was twined in such a way that we couldn't untangle it. Then the soldiers came with some sort of shears and they freed this young man's hands. But as a counterfavour he had to swallow two bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you about something that you've given evidence about? You told us about wire around the wrists of a young man. And you had said that you tried to remove the wire when you were in the room of death. Was he the only person who had his wrists tied up in wire? Do you know if anybody else had?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's go back then to the JNA barracks. You say he had to swallow bullets. How long did you stay in the barracks themselves, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Until about 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us then how it was you left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We were all called to a kind of hall where there were a lot of women also. A captain first class arrived. I think he was dressed in some sort of coat, not even a marshal would have such a coat. He was very decently dressed, and he said the following, "All of the Croats stay where you are, and everyone else should cross to the other side." And. A woman asked a silly question. She said, "And what am I, my husband is a Serb and I am a Croat." He replied, "You decide." She went to join the women, but I don't know which ones. And then he said -- he introduced himself, "I am Captain Vojin Misic, a Serb from Negoslavci. We will kill all of you, you hear? Burn you, set you on fire, and completely erase your Croatian seed by throwing your ashes into the Danube."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did you think when that was said to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: First of all, I thought if this was a normal person and was he really considering doing something like that. Still, he should have adhered to military rules and regulations. Ultimately he didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what did he do?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Nothing. He insulted us, cursed us and then a bus was brought. We were getting ready to board the bus and getting ready to go to the last detention camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is your neck all right? I see you --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It's all right. I'm adjusting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just deal, please, with -- and I will move on in time. I think it's right to say that you went to Sremska Mitrovica; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you got there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: First we passed through the last Croatian village, that was Tovarnik, and then we entered Sid. We waited there for quite a while; I don't know why. Then we set off. We arrived at Sremska Mitrovica. We came to the main square. The sports hall is close by. The driver stopped. Officers of the JNA came to look at us and to insult us. They ranged from the rank of major to the rank of colonel. They told us all sorts of things such as, "We would like to let you go, but Tudjman doesn't want you, so now we have to take care of you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with how you were treated at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We came to the entrance. After we left that first place where we stopped in Mitrovica, we came to the actual prison in Mitrovica. It was the prison where people who had been sentenced and convicted would serve out their sentence. We were going in through a pretty narrow entrance. You would go to that entrance and then you would have to step three or four steps down in order to get to the floor. And that's where they were waiting for us, police officers, dressed in police uniforms immediately started to beat us. These were not military police officers, but just regular police officers. They beat us, we were running, running until we reached a plateau. They asked us there one by one, there were two people there. One of them spoke in a Bosnian accent. I don't know what the other person was. He didn't really talk much. This first man was saying, "What's your name, my name is so-and-so, what did you do. I did this and that." And then he would say, "Oh, that's what you did. You were killing Serbs," and so on and so forth. This went on for some time. Then we were sent to the sports hall. I remember one police officer in a blue uniform. One of the doors was not working properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Forgive me for interrupting. I just want to stop your evidence at that place, if I may. I would like to deal now with one or two other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I make application to go into private session for a short period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you look at this document, please, which is dated the 13th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, to assist the Court, there are two documents here. There is the original in B/C/S and there is an English document. The English document which may assist the Court is number 00320180. I don't know if the Court can locate that or not. Well, perhaps it might assist the Court if I just deal with the original and then we can deal with the translation, we can do it one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, would you be kind enough to have a look at that document, the hard copy, as it is now called, to your left-hand side? Perhaps he can be shown that, please. It's not really necessary to put it on the ...

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I think it's right to say that --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: These are the results of my medical tests, the first ones after I left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, there is an English translation. I'm entirely in the Court's hands. I call out the number. It's a 65 ter number -- I think it's number 1 -- number 7. It should be number 7. The number is 00320180.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, if you will forgive us for the delay. It's one of the benefits of the electronic system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't wish to take up any more time. I don't know if it's going to be possible or not. It is an English translation. I certainly don't have it. Well, I will work on the assumption that the Court has a copy of it. Your Honour, I would seek to make the original B/C/S version an exhibit and attach to it the English translation, which I was not going to go into any great detail. The witness has already given evidence about knees and the vertebrae. Merely to draw the Court's attention to the bi-directional X-rays of both knees and then the subsequent analysis of the cervical vertebral column, the thoracic vertebral column and the lumbo-sacral vertebral column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We appear now to have the B/C/S, in part, on screen. There is certainly in the system the English version, but it's not yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just put it this way: May I make an application for it to be made as an exhibit. The witness has already given evidence about damage to knees and all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, you've made mention of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The B/C/S version with the English translation will be received as two parts of the one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be exhibit number 266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That being the case, those are all the questions that I would seek to ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cakalic, Mr. Vasic will now have some questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good day to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Cakalic. First of all, I wish to ask you something. Seeing that we both speak the same language, please make a brief pause after my question so that the interpreters can interpret my question and your response. In that way everybody else in the courtroom will be able to follow. First, I wish to clarify some technical matters in connection with your statements and then we'll move on to other matters. You have made a number of statements and you have testified in a number of proceedings, so let us see whether we have all these statements. On the 18th of March, 1992 you made a statement which bears number VU-BOL, meaning hospital, -46. Do you recall that and to whom did you make this statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me to whom it is addressed and I can comment on it, but I don't remember it, I'm sure I made the statement if you have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to move a little closer to the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will have it shown to you, and you can just glance at it briefly. Could the usher would assist. This statement is typed out, but it is stated here that you wrote it in your own hand, so please could you tell us: Have you seen it in this typed version?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I made this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't see my signature anywhere though. Oh, yes, I see now. It says that it was handwritten by me. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to take care not to overlap so as to not create confusion for the interpreters. You can lay this aside now. The next statement is addressed to the medical centre for human rights in Zagreb and bears the date the 18th of March, 1992. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the institution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Of course. It's addressed to the medical centre for human rights in Zagreb. And the date it bears is the 18th of March, 1992. The place is Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: If I signed it, then I certainly gave that statement, but I don't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could the usher please show it to the witness? And you will see in the last passage it says: "This statement is given of my own free will, Emil Cakalic, born on," and so on and so forth. If you could look at the third -- or, rather, the last page.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I accept this statement. It's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can lay it aside now too. On the 16th of May, 1992 you spoke to the representatives of the MUP of Croatia, the Vukovar police administration operations department, and an official note was drawn up by a MUP employee and he signed the statement, not you. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, sir, but I have to see the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Could the usher assist? Do you see on page 1 your name and on the last the fact that this official note was signed by a MUP employee, not by you? What I wish to know is whether this official note was drawn up after an interview with you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can lay it aside.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't like making unsigned statements, so because I did not sign this statement I do not abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the contents right now, just whether this is what it says it is. And then we'll come to the content later. Then on the 6th of March, 1993 you spoke to a lady who was a lieutenant-colonel of the Canadian army, and her name was Kim Carter?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of this interview of yours, a transcript was drawn up, which I assume you were shown?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was that 1993? 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 6th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The 6th of March, 1993. Yes, and Mr. Snow, Clyde was also present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this you were examined as a witness before the district court in Zagreb on the 10th of June, 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a judge from Sarengrad, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And this was the case against Slavko Dokmanovic and others?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, it's not the document I'm thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will show you this document also; it's not a problem. Could the usher please help?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was living in Samobor at the time. I went everywhere and didn't find accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement which you made as a witness?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those were things we mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can lay it aside. And then you spoke with the investigators of the OTP in The Hague, and on the 18th of June, 1995 you made your first statement to them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Could you please show it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then you had something to add on the 21st of April, 1996, something to add to that statement. I will show you both these documents. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that on the 5th of February, 1998 you testified before this Court in the case against Dokmanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you testified in another case before this Tribunal, and that was on the 16th of July, 2003 in the case against Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, against Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that -- or I have to say before that, on the 10th of July, 1993 you spoke to members of the MUP, the police administration in Kastel and they drew up an official note?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then the investigating judge of the War Crimes Chamber of the district court in Belgrade asked that you make a statement in Zagreb before a prosecutor from Belgrade and that was in April 2004?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that, on the 25th of September, 2004 you testified --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, October.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before the war crimes chamber in Belgrade, and there is a transcript in existence?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have another statement here made by you, which is signed, and it has a heading, Emil Cakalic, but there is no date, and it doesn't say to whom the statement was made. Would you please take a look at it and tell us, if you can, when you made it and to whom? Do you see on the front page it says "Emil Cakalic," and if you look at the last page there is a signature there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature, and it is my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell us when you made this statement and to whom you sent it, if you sent it to anyone?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I made this statement, but I don't know to whom I sent it -- I don't know who asked it of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when you made it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that either. I have a poor head for dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if now is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Vasic, and we will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I'm going to continue with my questions. You said that you worked at the hospital for a while. Can you tell us whether that was from 1968 to 1978? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, for 10 years. For 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you began to work at the Vukovar municipal office as a sanitary inspector. I assume that you were sanitation inspector for the entire region of Vukovar, including all the villages that were part of that municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just waiting for the interpretation to be completed.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We've already heard from other witnesses that the Vukovar area was multi-ethnic and that all the ethnic groups or all the peoples lived harmoniously in this area. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statements you mention the 2nd of May, 1991 and the events in Borovo Selo. This was the topic of the testimony here by a number of people. What I would like to know is if you, with the Vukovar municipal delegation and also people from the federal government, did you visit Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was at the head of a team that went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember after the events in Borovo Selo, were barricades erected in the villages with a majority Serb population as well as those with a majority Croat population facing the Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I know that Pacetin, Bobota, Negoslavci, Trpinja, Vera, some other places. I know that barricades were erected in these villages. I passed through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the situation similar in Borovo Naselje in relation to Trpinja and Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I heard that there was a barricade erected near the Dom Teknika [phoen], technology hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Actually, it was a little bit lower down in the direction of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since it was part of your duties to carry out sanitation inspections, you were also in contact with the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, I had a special person at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after these events in May that some special measures were introduced at the Vukovar Hospital, that they were given the tasks of preparing the hospital resources for a possible beginning of the conflict and to prepare for dealing with the wounded? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time that I'm hearing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You worked at the Vukovar municipal office in May, June, July, August. What I would like to know is what were the relations between the Vukovar authorities in the municipal assembly at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't a deputy in the municipal assembly, so I couldn't really tell you about that. But I could tell you what the relations were amongst us as colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Serbian people felt threatened and you know from where -- from when.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, tell us.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: From July when a gentleman came to Vukovar from Sibenik. I think you know who I mean. His last name evades me at the moment. Dr. -- Dr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the gentleman employed at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he work the at the Sibenik hospital. He was a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he a Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it Dr. Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Raskovic, I remember now. In July Dr. Raskovic came to Vukovar, and this was something that pleased many Serbs. I think he made a mistake in coming there because he incited the Serb people in Vukovar to rebellion, and this is why what happened in Vukovar happened. As I said, I had a weekend house or a little holiday house in a resort, and I could hear everything from across the Vuka. I could hear everything that they were saying from the other side of the Vuka because the microphones were so powerful. There was a rally of Serbs. I practically attended this rally. I wasn't there physically, but I could hear everything that was going on. But if you were to ask me exactly what was happening, I could no longer tell you anything about it, but you know very well what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about that. What I would like to ask you is the following: You said that the Serbs felt threatened from July. What was the specific reason for that; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that the Serbs were in danger from July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, you said they felt endangered.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a different thing. They felt threatened. I assume, I don't know, but I assume when Dr. Raskovic left they felt as if they had been put on the spot. These were my colleagues, so instead of continuing to socialise -- well, if you can imagine, if any of my colleagues had come to Vukovar and talked against the Serbs, I would be upset. I would be angry. Why? Because we were people who had more or less the same training, went to the same schools, had the same hobbies, went fishing together. So then after a certain amount of time it's not proper to do things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell us whether from June onwards any measures or activities were undertaken in Vukovar which were not usual or regular activities? For example, in the domain of civilian protection and the people's defence department?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The people's defence department operated in accordance with its principles and tasks and regulations. I assume everything was all right. It was working. If something was not working, then that's not all right. Can you please put a direct question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it true on the 15th of June, 1991 you joined some activities by the then organisation of the defence of Vukovar which later grew into the Vukovar army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I did this on a voluntary basis because -- I have to tell you. Why are you going to listen to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Because I saw that some things vis-a-vis hygiene were not functioning, food was being made for a school in a yard, and things like that. So I volunteered to oversee these duties. I was told to do these jobs and I did them well. I organised a central point where all the food supplies were made and issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what sort of a system this was, this food organisation supply system, how did that work?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The main centre was the worker's hall. It's in the centre of town. There's a large kitchen there. I was overseeing the work there, and I can say that Serbs, Croats, and some others were all working there. They worked excellently, and they worked very well. The husband and wife who were Serbs never prompted me to make any kind of remarks about their work. They even worked better than the others, but actually if all of the others heard me saying that they worked better, they might be upset because they all worked very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure they won't be angry. In any case, how was the food distributed from this workers' hall, and in that period, July, August and September, who was it issued to?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We did it for as long as we could, until a part of the workers' hall was destroyed. That's where food for the Croatian army was prepared in special Thermos containers. They were quite large. I requested that these vessels be used because that was the only way that the flask was opened only when they were going to eat. And they all had to eat together. It shouldn't have been opened one by one, that was bad, and it could pose some danger, so I always looked at things from the point of view of health. This food was distributed by the army, taken to certain places in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who controlled the food quality and who took care that this food supply system was protected from sabotage?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: All of those who tried the food also -- all those who prepared the food tasted it, so that's how it was done. Food was also prepared at the hotel Vukovar for the police and also for a number of other employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the Dunav Hotel?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've said that you volunteered in June 1991. Can you tell us who did you go to to volunteer, who assigned you for this duty?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I said that I went to the defence department, to the special services department, which was a part of that. It was a gentleman who, in the meantime, has died. I went to him, and I said I would like to volunteer for the Croatian army in order to prepare and control the food, drinking water and all the other activities that had to do with this kind of work. Did your inspectors also report in the same way? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know. Can you please tell us whether at the time Tomislav Mercep was already at the head of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were given this assignment in June was he at -- in charge of preparations for the defence of Vukovar? And if not, do you know who it was?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: All of those working at the secretariat were working on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time under a decision of the Croatian government was the Vukovar municipal assembly dismissed and was Mr. Marin Vidic appointed in that function?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The assembly was not working when Mr. Dokmanovic disappeared, when he left the area. I don't know where he went. I think he crossed the Danube to go to the other side or was living in Bobota; I don't know. But in any case, yes. What I said before is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is that in June was the Crisis Staff of the Vukovar municipality already formed at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this was in July or later. I really am not able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course we will not insist on dates if you cannot recall them. Do you know -- how are you feeling? If you are having any problems, please let us know. Do you know who comprised the Vukovar municipality Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't like to guess. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You didn't attend the Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. I was just doing my job, what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have frequent contacts with Mr. Marin Vidic during July and August?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume that the contacts had to do with your work that you had started doing in June. What I would like to know is if you knew what the duties were of Mr. Vidic during those two months, July and August?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was entrusted by the Croatian government for the area of Vukovar. So he was the commissioner of the government of Croatia for the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he performing only the duties that he would be performing as president of the municipality regularly, or was he doing something that had to do with the activities of the Crisis Staff in making preparations for the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was part of the Crisis Staff. We went to Borovo Naselje together. We lived through rocket explosions, shelling, grenade explosions. It was a clearing, cleared area outside of Vukovar, but thank God we survived. We were taken there by a driver. He had to go back to lunch, and he also had to take some fuel somewhere. Unfortunately, he was hit by a shell and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Mr. Mercep?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, you mentioned Mr. Mercep.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I mentioned him. As far as I know, he also wasn't a professional soldiers. He wasn't a soldier by profession?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, he was a construction engineer, civil construction engineer, and that's what he is to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that he ran the Vukovar defence until Mr. Dedakovic came, who was a professional soldier, and this was sometime in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I assume that as were you carrying out your duties already from August onwards, you had contacts not only with Mr. Marin Vidic, Bili, but also with the Vukovar defence command since you were in charge of checking the food, which was later distributed to the army or to the soldiers; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how often you went to the Vukovar defence staff and where was it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was opposite from the municipal billing in a side street. Do you know where that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: You asked me whether I went to the command. No, I had instructions from my commander to do such and such a thing and so on, and then when Mr. Dedakovic came, he called me to see him. We spoke outside in the yard, and he said to me, "Inspector, you need to do these things, such and such things, such and such a thing." And I told him, "Well, I've already been doing that for a while." And that's how these contacts actually ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that you were actually just performing your professional duties, so there was no need to actually discuss that in detail?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have the same relationship after Mr. Dedakovic left Vukovar and was succeeded by Mr. Borkovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Branko. But this was already well into the conflict, and I don't know, once I was at the municipal building, there was shelling, I couldn't leave, so I spent the night there. I think Branko was there also. We spoke but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since you were monitoring the food quality, could you please tell us something about the quantities of food and how many soldiers were receiving this food in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many soldiers there were, but I ordered that the food that was not eaten by the soldiers had to be given to the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume that the food was distributed in the shelters in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I ordered that no food should be wasted. It was wartime. If the soldiers did not take all the food, it had to be given to whoever was hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said that you went to the hospital ex officio and that there was a contact person there. When you went to the hospital, did you see wounded JNA soldiers there who were imprisoned and kept under guard?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them. I did see members of the ZNG who had been killed, however. But this is the first time I've heard about what you're mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know there were JNA hospitals [as interpreted] In the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do know that they were taken prisoner and that they were patients in the hospital. And on the day when we were arrested and taken away on that day they were sent somewhere. I don't know where. I think they were sent back to Sremska Mitrovica. No, it was a lieutenant who was sent back to Sremska Mitrovica. I do know that they were given back, but I never found out where they actually went.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a correction of the transcript. Page 66, line 22. My question was: You didn't know that there were JNA soldiers in the hospital, and here it says there were JNA hospitals. It's an error in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Has that got to do with me? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, no, it has nothing to do with you. What I said was not properly interpreted. Tell me, where were you when you were not touring the terrain?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: At home. I went to work for as long as I was able. In July, that's when I did this work, but afterwards, when one could no longer go anywhere, I was ordered to stay at home and to report, if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your house was in the immediate vicinity of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was not my house; it was an apartment block. There were three buildings. They all looked the same. They were only different colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did tell us that. What I want to know is how far from the hospital was your flat or how far from the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies or the normal route?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, the route you used.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I took a shortcut and I used the long way as well. As the crow flies, about 400 metres. But that's approximate. I never measured it, so I can't really tell you the precise number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, when you were carrying out your assignments, there were ZNG units, were there, and you were a member because you were doing this job?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the process of being organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Apart from the tasks you carried out in quality control --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- Did you do any other work that had to do with civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the Red Cross. I was the president of the municipal Red Cross committee of Vukovar. I had been for about 10 years. I was a member of other humanitarian organisations as well. I have received many awards for that work, but when I came back to Vukovar, I didn't find a single one of them. Somebody else is now displaying these.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were heading the Karitas [phoen] and the Red Cross. Who appointed you to that duty and when did you stop holding this post?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was elected by the assembly of the Red Cross which reappointed me. And could you repeat the second part of your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the summer and autumn of 1991, were you the president of the Red Cross branch in Vukovar and until when?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, for as long as I was able. To, and when I left the camp we founded the Red Cross in exile in Zagreb, and I was again elected president.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who, besides you, was in the presidency of the Red Cross branch in Vukovar at the relevant time, August, September, October, November 1991?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The secretary, her husband, Slobodan Maricic -- it fell apart, you know. As the war progressed, the society fell apart. The secretary left the Red Cross and she went off somewhere, so that I appointed a lady to be the secretary of the Red Cross, and the assembly could no longer meet, but as the president I had the right to appoint her, and she did a good job. She did a good job, for all the inhabitants of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the name of this lady?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Zeljka Zgonjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, you said that you volunteered to join, and that at that time the defenders of the town could join up voluntarily. When was their general mobilisation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was at home and some lads arrived and they asked me how old I was. And I said why, and they said, "So we can mobilise you." This was a few days before Vukovar fell, when they went from the houses collecting people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were they from the municipal Crisis Staff or from the defence staff?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That was the first time I had seen those lads, when they came to my door.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in Vukovar were there volunteers from other parts of Croatia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember from what places to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Zagreb, Sisak, Medjimurje. There were very many volunteers in Vukovar. It wasn't only people from Vukovar who defended Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, apart from the volunteers who came to defend Vukovar, certain MUP units also arrived from other towns of Croatia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, not a single formation that arrived was ever designated as coming from this or that place. They were always called the defenders of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you knew they were not natives of Vukovar because you didn't know them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I didn't know everybody from Vukovar. Although I moved around a lot, I didn't know everyone. There were 20.000 workers in Borovo. Who could know them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether certain parties, such as the Croatian Party of Rights sent their members in units of the Croatian defence forces to defend Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were a few of those. But they quickly vanished from there. I don't know whether they were killed, but there were very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When answering my learned friend's questions you said that you carried out your tasks on the ground and spent the rest of the time at home until the 17th or 18th -- until the 17th of November, 1991. But I would like to know when on the 17th of November you left your flat and went to the hospital, did you already know that the Vukovar Hospital was about to be evacuated by ships on the Danube to Hungary?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I heard about that in the hospital. I left my flat on the 17th, and two soldiers were going towards the entrance, and I said, "Lads, where are you off to?" And then we had a chat and we parted ways. They were children, you know. Children. I think you know why I'm saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about conscripts who could not be older than 19?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's not in the transcript. There was a law that you had to go to the army when you were 18?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What did you hear in the hospital and from whom concerning this evacuation which was to take place by the Danube?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I only heard rumours. Somebody said there will be an evacuation, but it didn't happen. Somebody said it, but there were several of us in a room, and I don't know who said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't the reason you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. I felt that this was a humanitarian institution which should not be touched, although it had been touched. You know that a 200-kilogram shell landed between somebody's legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we've heard that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. And he's still alive. I'm speaking of that projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And we were told that he was a Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he was by ethnicity. I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On your arrival in the hospital, did you have to report your arrival to the hospital Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I did report. Dr. Vesna Bosanac was the director of the hospital, and she had to know who was coming into the hospital. She had to see. I reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that at first your wife could not get into the hospital. Did I understand you correctly that the civilians who had gathered there could get into the hospital yard, but not the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, I intervened. I told her to wait outside and she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, when you arrived in the hospital and reached the room, the X-ray department --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- was Mr. Guncevic already there and the other gentlemen you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Guncevic came after I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Ivankovic at the time, who worked in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And his son too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You knew him and his son from before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because I used to work in the hospital. I met his son at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. His son's name is Goran?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in view of the fact that you were a member of the Red Cross, the president of the --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was a volunteer. And it was the municipal organisation and the association of municipalities of Slavonia and Baranja. I was president of that, too, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in October of 1991 there was a convoy from Vukovar Hospital and that some wounded were sent in the direction of Vinkovac and then on to Zagreb? This was on the 17th of October, 1991. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I think they were supposed to go, but then they didn't manage to get through. However, I don't remember. I'm not sure. I don't think they managed to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse you, but according to what we've heard from witnesses, there were two convoys; one on the 13th of October, which didn't get through from the barracks to the hospital because of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, now you've jogged my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the other one was on the 17th of October, which did go to Zagreb with a certain number of wounded?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, I remember now. Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know how medical supplies were distributed for the hospital or did you not deal with that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, it was other services that dealt with that, not me. But let me tell you, I got chlorine from the hospital pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, I was just about to ask you that. I was going to ask you where you got the chemicals indispensable for your activity?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I got those materials from that pharmacy and other pharmacies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, were medicines and other chemicals brought into Vukovar by helicopters for a while which landed in the Sloga stadium close to your flat?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard those stories, but I never saw it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were in charge of your tasks in Vukovar but not in Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was in Borovo Naselje, together with Vidic. Vidic and I went there together to solve some problems. And after that I didn't go to Borovo Naselje until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you were not tasked with that area?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, no, it was others who were. It was very difficult to get there, you know. I think that this happened sometime in early November and there was shooting all over the place. We were lucky that our car was not hit by a single shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if a part of the food prepared in these kitchens, was it delivered to the castle of Count Eltz? Were there any units there that received food from there? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I didn't go there. I had my own routes that I covered for as long as I could. I didn't go to the castle. It was exposed to a lot of shelling, heavy shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to allow my learned friend Mr. Moore the 15 minutes that he had asked for to discuss some issues, and then I will continue my cross-examination tomorrow, if you think that that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it 15 minutes, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I would have thought five minutes would see us through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Five minutes. What about another five minutes or so, Mr. Vasic, and then we will call it an interim day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just didn't want to think that -- I didn't want to allow my -- I didn't want my learned friend to think that I was not allowing enough time for him to deal with what he wanted to deal with. Anyway, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before the 17th of November when you went to the hospital, did you see members of the ZNG in front of the hospital guarding the yard and the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, but I did see dead ones. I said that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that there were plenty of dead in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the reason for that is that for a time it was impossible to bury the dead at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We had problems with that in Vukovar. I came to the cemetery where people of all ethnic groups were buried, and as soon as they saw that someone else is there, they started shooting. I even saw a person who was living in a four-storey house would be giving the signal when they should open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that you didn't see any security staff of the hospital. Were there any people who were guarding the hospital? That would be normal, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would be, but I didn't really enter the hospital so often. There was a team there that was performing certain duties. I was at the hospital only on one occasion, and that was two days before it was captured. That's when I was there. I could see everything was functioning there, everything was all right. A colleague of mine was working there. He was also a sanitation inspector, so he was the one who took up these duties there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you went to the municipal building, or rather to that part where the Crisis Staff was, to these meetings or consultations with Mr. Vidic, you had to pass by the MUP, the Vukovar MUP?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I went for one conversation with Mr. Vidic. So I went to see him on one occasion. And then we went to Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether of your family it was just you and your wife who came to the hospital, or did anyone else from your family also go there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, it was just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Once you came to the hospital did you see Mr. Dragutin Berghofer there whom you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we went to Ovcara together from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see any ZNG members at the hospital whom you knew, if you can remember. If not --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Only those who brought in the sick had access to the hospital, and the hospital staff had access. Until the 17th, approximately. There was a person at the entrance who was posted at the entrance; I don't know anything much about that. Dr. Bosanac was the director at the hospital, so this was her job. I never interfered in anyone else's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the 17th when you came to that building, did you see any people whom you knew were members of the ZNG, but who were no longer in uniform, but were in civilian clothes or white coats or anything like that? Did you see people like that or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of people in the hospital. They were all looking for shelter, so it was either a shelter or the hospital. The shelters were so packed. The hospital also was very crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, should we stop now and deal with the questions by my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Sir, the Chamber is about to adjourn for the day, and we'll continue tomorrow commencing at 2.15 in the afternoon. We have a procedural matter or two to deal with now, but rather than keep you there, it will be, I think, preferable for you to be able to leave now, and if you could return in time for your evidence to continue at 2.15 tomorrow. The court officer will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's really three small matters. Firstly, in respect of the agreed facts, the facts have been agreed on all matters with one exception. That relates to the suggestion that the Prosecution say can be demonstrated on documents, that the grave was located, I think, on the 18th of October, 1992. I think there is only one of my learned friends who may object to that. I think it is my learned friend Mr. Borovic. I hope he can agree it, because if not I'm going to have to ask to call additional witnesses for that matter. And I cannot, for the life of me think that it goes to any issue that needs to be determined by this Tribunal. I don't say it by way of criticism, but perhaps if we can just clarify it now, I would be very grateful. That is the first matter. The second matter is as a result of the unfortunate death of Mr. Milosevic, we of course have been keeping afternoon court invariably four days out of five. I know my learned friends and myself would prefer to have morning sessions, if at all possible, and we would respectfully ask the Court if that could be considered sooner rather than later, but I know that there are other considerations to come into play. And I know that Your Honour in particular has certain obligations as a result of that eventuality. The third matter is, as a result of the Milosevic trial, if I may use that phrase, not being effective, I think Mr. Borovic and myself agreed that if the Court were minded, we would be prepared with of course the others, to have double sessions for one or two weeks to make up the time. And for our part, we have witnesses that we can call. If that was to be done, it would affect our scheduling, because if we are running from 9.00 until 7.00, clearly we have to bring in witnesses well in advance. And I really just ask the Court to consider that. I know Mr. Borovic was keen for that particular course. Those are the three matters that I would wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Borovic, on the agreed fact, is there any clarification you can give at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am hearing about this problem for the first time. We had discussed it, my learned friend and I, so -- we actually did not discuss it. This is the first time that I'm hearing of it. So I do not wish to give any comments about that until I discuss that with my colleagues. As far as the schedule is concerned, I am all for completing this trial as soon as possible, so whatever we can do to facilitate that, I would be very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Borovic and Mr. Moore, ensure that attention is given to the question of the agreed fact between you in the hope that it can be resolved during this week? Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Borovic. As will be apparent -- Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The first item as far as that's concerned, you've already instructed what the sides are to do. Regarding the change of schedule to the morning, the Defence teams are in favour of that because it's easier to work in the morning, if possible. As far as the third matter is concerned, what I would like to tell the Trial Chamber is a problem that my client has, and then it becomes my problem too regarding this proposal. You know that my client had two heart surgeries before he surrendered voluntarily to the Tribunal, and this pace of trial continuously for the past two months, five days a week, is quite intense for him, so he has complained to me recently of fatigue and the difficulties he has following the proceedings in the courtroom. In such circumstances, working double shifts would create additional problems for him. But I would like for the Trial Chamber to hear my client's opinion of this whole matter so that you would hear it firsthand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, thank you. I won't call on Mr. Lukic at the moment, not out of rudeness, but to say a few words which may assist all counsel. Because of the unexpected circumstances, it clearly will be possible for there to be some rearrangement of the listings of the existing trials that are presently being conducted. That will be something that will be subject to adjustment and review as other trial or trials are brought on stream in place of the trial that has terminated unexpectedly and as other decisions are given. Clearly there is need for the President to reconsider a number of factors about the future trial listings and the disposition of judges. It is therefore not appropriate immediately to take steps which will depend for their effectiveness upon matters that have to be considered by the President. Certainly where there are morning courts available, as has been indicated by the Chamber, it too is human, and it too feels the strain of late evening sittings. There are, however, still at the moment only two courtrooms available, and there are a number of other factors, including already committed times which will tie up members of the Chamber during this week because of other commitments, and in my case, extending into next week. So that just because there is a court available in the morning, it doesn't mean that the Chamber is free to sit then. The Chamber has, in the past, sat for extended periods in a day. Two or three members of the Chamber have sat on occasions from 7.00 until 9.00 at night; on one case in the morning and another in the afternoon. It is the experience of the judges, and it is the experience of other Chambers that to do that other than on one day for some exceptional reason produces undesirable strain on counsel, on Judges, on accused, and on witnesses, and especially on witnesses who are not at all used to this sort of regime. It was the experience of this Chamber that sitting any longer than from 10.00 to about 4.30 or a little later, with a full lunch break, for more than two or three days, produced too great a strain. It also has long-term staffing problems with interpreters, security personnel and the like. Therefore, while we will certainly consider, as soon as our conflicting commitments are resolved, the possibility if there are courtrooms available, of starting at a slightly later time and sitting through into the afternoon. It would be quite undesirable, and I think harmful for a number of reasons, including what Mr. Vasic has mentioned, to contemplate sitting day after day from 9.00 in the morning until 7.00 at night. As soon as some of the uncertainties are resolved, I hope that there can be some revision of our present trial schedule. But the factors that I've mentioned will be taken into account and will guide what we do. Thank you. We will now adjourn and resume at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of March, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
